claims.text: Conventionally powder-metallurgy-produced W–Cu composites, including those made by spark-plasma sintering, suffer from phase separation and void formation.
Applying a thin, Cu-affinitive vapor-deposited interlayer to W particles or regions will enhance W–Cu wetting and bonding during consolidation.
A vapor-deposited interlayer will promote nearly perfect interfacial contact between W and Cu.
The pre-coating will reduce voids and phase separation in W–Cu composites.
The coated W–Cu composite will preserve mechanical durability under reactor irradiation conditions.
Spark-plasma sintering can be used to consolidate powder-derived alloy materials.
The vapor-deposited interlayer creates a chemically continuous W–Cu interface.
The vapor-deposited interlayer creates a structurally continuous W–Cu interface.
Improved wetting by molten or diffusing Cu during sintering produces a more uniform W–Cu microstructure with fewer defects.
Reducing W–Cu interfacial defects enhances thermal transport across the interface.
A chemically and structurally continuous W–Cu interface enhances mechanical load transfer.
The proposed interfacial improvements will persist under irradiation.
Relative to otherwise comparable uncoated composites, coated samples will have higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to otherwise comparable uncoated composites, coated samples will retain or improve compressive yield strength.
Relative to uncoated composites, coated samples will have a more defect-free W–Cu interface.
Induction casting, arc-plasma casting, and uncoated spark-plasma sintering tend to produce W–Cu phase separation, voids, and thermal-transport-limiting defects.
